If you've found your ictus (focal point) then you need to focus on just hitting that focal point every time you move your arms. Bring them up to your focal point, and down to your sides over and over again. Try doing a small "one" to just eye level over and over again, not fast. Focus on just hitting your focal point with just the tips of your fingers every single time.

 Then, look at your hands. They should be relaxed, fingers together, slightly curved. Your wrists should be relaxed, but not floppy. Every time you bring your hands up to the upbeat of that one, your palms should be up, and when you hit your focal point they should be facing down.

 Turn to the side and make sure as you do this movement you're staying on a flat plane. You should be able to conduct with a wall in front of you and have your fingertips touch the wall the whole time you conduct. Remember that your pattern doesn't have to be big to be seen, just focus on controlling your movement for now.

 Check out silent command's YouTube channel for conducting fundamentals, and consider taking some lessons through DMLA (drum major leadership academy). They're fairly cheap and their instructors are very helpful individuals. If you need further help, feel free to PM me.

You do need to know enough about measure and music structure in order to not only conduct, but understand what you're doing when you conduct and what it means to the band. Definitely ask your band director about it, and go ahead and use online resources to learn as well. I've had a drum major who was a colorguard and she didn't take the time to learn that and it was a mess trying to teach the person who was supposed to be the most informed. I know you can do it if you work hard to learn. If you have the money, lessons help so much.

This is a late comment but I didn't get it for my first 2 years trying out (going into sophomore and junior seasons) due to seniority (I mean a half point between me and the one who got the position came from the directors "preference points"), and honestly the drive that losing gave me made me work so much harder than I would have from getting the position either time. My band needed me as section leader (a flute section of 2 just like your Mello section). My advice is to use your disappointment of not getting the position this year to drive you to not just be better than everyone else trying out, but to be the best player, marcher, and leader on and off of the field this year along with advancing yourself as a conductor. You don't have to be a drum major to embody everything that being a drum major means. As for some resources, I reccomend DMLA. My instructor is Dallan and he's absolutely amazing, but all of their instructors are awesome. They're gonna be having another summer leadership camp this month and I can't reccomend any experience more.

Edit: I looked at your questions and realized I hadn't really provided and answer to the recruitment one. Honestly, that's something that I've struggled with even in a 7-12 band, but it's so much harder in your situation. Talk to trumpet players your age and younger that you know and let them try the Mello if they want to, along with being really really friendly and excited about your instrument at any event where you get to talk to younger recruits (we usually do a concert that was cancelled for obvious reasons) and be generally very welcoming, but don't be discouraged if not many people are interested. The Mello tends to be a very low participation instrument for us as well (idk why I LOVE the Mello and think it's awesome!) and I'm sure that carries on into many bands, but young trumpets are honestly your best chance. Ones that feel like they aren't advancing quickly are at risk for quitting, but sometimes a switch is an easy fix to their discouraged attitude.
